scenario: AITA for not directly paying my friend for half of the gas used on a trip? | I will keep this short. We went on a trip and used two tanks of gas. 1 tank there and 1 tank back. I used my company gas card to fill up when we left our home city (the tank was on empty). When he went to fill up the tank on the way home he asked for half the money but I said no since I provided us with an entire tank to get to the destination. His argument was that since I didn't pay for it myself it didn't count, I think it does count since I still supplied us with half the tank and my method of acquiring the gas shouldn't matter. We did use his car but it shouldn't matter since we had used my car for the last trip which was roughly the same distance and it was his turn to provide the vehicle. AITA?

AITA for not directly paying my friend for half of the gas used on a trip? | I will keep this short. We went on a trip and used two tanks of gas. 1 tank there and 1 tank back. Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: I’ll answer with a **0** (not AITA, but with nuance). ### **Why?** Your perspective is reasonable, but the issue isn’t just about who "paid" for the gas—it’s about **shared responsibility, fairness, and communication**. Here’s why: 1. **You contributed half the fuel** – You provided the gas to reach the destination, which is a tangible contribution. If you’d used your own money to buy gas at the start, he’d likely agree it’s fair to split costs. Since you used a company card, the *intent* (covering the trip’s fuel) remains the same. 2. **His argument is flawed** – Saying "you didn’t pay for it yourself" ignores that you *did* cover the cost (via company funds) and that the gas was used equally by both of you. His turn to drive doesn’t negate the shared expense of fuel. 3. **But fairness requires compromise** – If you’re uncomfortable splitting the cost (e.g., company policy restricts reimbursement), you could: - Offer to cover his share in another way (e.g., a meal, future favor). - Agree to split the *next* trip’s fuel as a balance. - Clarify upfront how shared expenses will be handled to avoid future disputes. ### **Key Takeaway** You’re not *wrong* for refusing to split the cost, but his expectation is also understandable. The best approach is **open communication**—next time, discuss how to handle shared expenses beforehand. A **0** reflects that you’re not in the wrong, but the situation could be improved with better agreement. Would you like help drafting a message to resolve this amicably?
